core_obligations: The construction of the shift matrix at proof lines 687-689: the quantity U(n;z) is defined as Psi(n+1;z) Psi(n;z) inverse, which makes the first of the two announced equations a definition to be identified with a polynomial in z.

Analyticity at proof lines 690-691: since the jump condition for Psi does not depend on n, the difference of the two jumps cancels and U is analytic in the plane, so it is determined by its behaviour at infinity and at the origin alone.

The behaviour at infinity at proof lines 692-698: substituting the expansion of Psi at infinity and the diagonal normalization factors produces an expansion of U with a finite polynomial part of degree N-1 and a finite limit at infinity.

The behaviour at the origin at proof lines 699-709: substituting the behaviour of Psi at the origin produces a matrix T whose expansion has a pole of order N+1, so T times Psi has no singularity and the derivative equation is an identity of analytic functions.

The concluding expansion at proof lines 710-760: the two behaviours together give the displayed expansion of T(n;z) in powers of z from z to the power N-1 down to z to the power minus N-1, and the first coefficient is identified as theta_N over 2 times sigma_3, which is the displayed equation for T_1(n).
proof_roadmap: Define U(n;z) as Psi(n+1;z) Psi(n;z) inverse and note that it is analytic because the jump condition does not depend on n.
Expand U at infinity using the expansion of Psi, and read off its polynomial part and its limit.
Study the behaviour of the derivative equation at the origin to locate the pole of T.
Collect the two behaviours into the displayed expansion of T and identify its leading coefficient.
metadata.difficulty_reason: The statement is the article's Proposition environment at source lines 654-680: it announces the Lax pair of the discrete Painleve II hierarchy, that is the shift equation Psi(n+1;z) = U(n;z) Psi(n;z) together with the derivative equation in z with matrix T(n;z), and it records that the leading coefficient is T_1(n) equal to theta_N over 2 times sigma_3. The proof at source lines 686-760 is a substantive argument rather than a pointer. It constructs U explicitly as Psi(n+1;z) Psi(n;z) inverse (proof lines 687-689), shows that U is analytic because the jump condition for Psi does not depend on n (proof lines 690-691), substitutes the expansion of Psi at infinity to obtain the behaviour of U there (proof lines 692-698) and the behaviour at the origin to locate the pole of T of order N+1 (proof lines 699-709), and finishes by writing out the expansion of T in powers of z and identifying its leading coefficient (proof lines 710-760). The only step the reader must supply is the algebra of the two substitutions, which is displayed in full. The claim is H3 because the argument is a multi-step matrix computation in two asymptotic regimes whose output is the explicit expansion of T.

core_obligations: The explicit discrete equation at proof lines 891-905: substituting the definition of Phi into the shifted variable rewrites Phi(n+1;z) through the diagonal factors, the lower triangular factor carrying x_n and the wave function Psi evaluated at the square of the spectral variable.

The formation of the matrix M_n(z) at proof lines 906-952: composing the shifted expression with the inverse of Phi and using the derivative equation at the squared variable produces the displayed matrix M_n(z), whose entries are written out in full in the displayed formula labelled eq:M(n,z).

The vanishing of the trace at proof lines 954-958: using the value of the trace of T, the trace of M_n(z) is computed as minus two n plus two over z plus two z times the trace of T at the squared variable, which is zero, so the first of the two announced equations holds.

The rationality of the entries at proof lines 959-960: reading the displayed form of M_n(z) together with the explicit expansion of T shows that every entry of M_n(z) is a rational function of z, which is the second of the two announced properties.

Identification of the system at proof lines 891-962 as a whole: the two verified properties are exactly what the announced system of equations asserts about Phi, so the Proposition follows once both are established.
proof_roadmap: Write the shifted wave function Phi(n+1;z) explicitly from its definition.
Compose it with the inverse of Phi and use the derivative equation to obtain the matrix M_n(z).
Compute the trace of M_n(z) with the trace identity for T and check that it vanishes.
Read the displayed expression of M_n(z) together with the expansion of T to see that its entries are rational in z.

proof_spans.label: the author's own proof environment immediately following it (source lines 781-825)

standard_prerequisites.name: The Lax pair of the discrete Painleve II hierarchy
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Same article, the Proposition labelled Prop:LaxPair at source lines 654-680, delivered by this lane as material L18277
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies the derivative equation satisfied by the wave function Psi, which the proof differentiates at the inverted spectral variable.

standard_prerequisites.name: Symmetry of the solution of the Riemann-Hilbert problem
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Same article, the Corollary labelled eq:sym Y at source lines 508-518, not delivered on this card
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies the symmetry of Y under inversion of the spectral variable, from which the proof deduces the corresponding symmetry of the wave function Psi.

standard_prerequisites.name: The coefficients kappa_n and x_n of the orthogonal polynomials
standard_prerequisites.source_reference: Same article, the subsection at source lines 419-459 and the definition of the reflection coefficients used there
standard_prerequisites.use: Supplies the meaning of kappa_n and x_n appearing in the conjugating matrix K(n) and in the identity recorded in the intervening Remark.

core_obligations: The derivative of the wave function at the inverted variable at proof lines 782-784: applying the chain rule to the derivative equation of the Lax pair transforms the derivative in z of Psi(n;z inverse) into minus one over z squared times T at the inverted variable times Psi at the inverted variable.

The symmetry of the wave function at proof lines 785-800: the symmetry of Y at the inverted variable is transported to the wave function by multiplying the diagonal normalization factors, the matrix Y at the origin and its inverse, and the sigma_3 factor, in the order in which the wave function is assembled from them.

Substitution and comparison at proof lines 801-820: substituting the transported symmetry into the derivative identity of the first step and comparing with the derivative of the same expression computed directly produces the announced relation between T at the inverted variable and the conjugate of T at the variable by the matrix K(n).

Identification of the conjugating matrix at proof lines 764-774 and 801-820: the matrix K(n) built from Y at the origin, the diagonal matrix of kappa_n and sigma_3 is exactly the matrix appearing in the comparison, so the displayed symmetry holds with that K(n).
The closing remark inside the proof lines 815-824: the two sides are brought to the displayed common form, which is the announced symmetry, and the argument stops there.
proof_roadmap: Differentiate the wave function at the inverted spectral variable with the derivative equation of the Lax pair.
Transport the symmetry of Y to the wave function Psi.
Substitute the transported symmetry into the derivative identity and compare both sides.
Read off the conjugating matrix K(n) and conclude the displayed symmetry.
metadata.difficulty_reason: The statement is the article's Proposition environment at source lines 764-775: the Lax matrix T satisfies T(n;z inverse) equal to minus z squared times the difference between the conjugate of T by the matrix K(n) and n over z times the identity, with K(n) displayed explicitly in terms of Y at the origin, the diagonal matrix of kappa_n and sigma_3. The proof at source lines 781-825 is a real two-sided computation and it is displayed in full: it differentiates the wave function at the inverted variable by the derivative equation of the Lax pair (proof lines 782-784), transports the symmetry of Y to the wave function by multiplying the same factors through which the wave function is built (proof lines 785-800), and then compares the two expressions to produce the displayed relation and to identify the conjugating matrix (proof lines 801-820).
